reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A rapidly growing mycobacterium widely distributed in water, causing predominantly skin, soft-tissue, and post-procedural infection
Disseminated cutaneous disease with multiple nodules on the limbs is characteristic in immunosuppressed patients, especially those on corticosteroids or after solid-organ transplantation
Associated with outbreaks linked to tattoo ink, mesotherapy, injections, and contaminated water, and with catheter-related infection
A recognised cause of keratitis following laser refractive and other eye surgery
Unlike some rapid growers it usually lacks a functional inducible macrolide-resistance gene and is often macrolide-susceptible, with tobramycin frequently more active than amikacin
Pulmonary disease is much less common than with M. abscessus
Management combines susceptibility-guided macrolide-based multidrug therapy with surgical debridement and removal of any infected foreign material
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium chelonae is an environmental rapidly growing mycobacterium found in water supplies. Disease usually follows percutaneous inoculation through trauma, surgery, injection, or contaminated solutions and devices, producing localised nodules and abscesses. In immunocompetent hosts infection tends to remain localised, whereas impaired cell-mediated immunity, particularly corticosteroid therapy and transplantation, predisposes to disseminated cutaneous disease with crops of nodules and to deeper infection. The organism forms biofilms on catheters and prosthetic material, and its relatively preserved susceptibility to macrolides distinguishes it from the more resistant M. abscessus.
additionalDifferentials: Other rapidly growing mycobacteria (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum)
Disseminated fungal infection with cutaneous nodules
additionalInvestigations: Culture of skin or tissue showing rapid mycobacterial growth
Molecular speciation to distinguish it from other rapid growers
Drug-susceptibility testing including macrolides, tobramycin, and amikacin
Skin biopsy for histology and staining
Assessment of immune status and medication review in disseminated disease
Corneal scrape and culture in suspected post-surgical keratitis
redFlags: Disseminated cutaneous nodules indicating impaired cell-mediated immunity
Catheter-related or prosthesis-related infection requiring device removal
Progressive infection despite apparently appropriate therapy
reference.prognosis: Localised infection in immunocompetent hosts generally responds well to combined medical and surgical treatment. Disseminated disease in immunosuppressed patients requires prolonged therapy and reduction of immunosuppression where possible, and outcomes depend on the underlying condition; relapse can occur if infected foreign material is not removed.
pitfalls: Assuming the drug-resistance pattern of M. abscessus and withholding a potentially effective macrolide
Continuing immunosuppression unchanged in disseminated disease
Treating device-associated infection without removing the device
Missing a common contaminated injection or cosmetic-procedure source in clustered cases
